The Sundanese gamelan degung of West Java features instruments, scales, and repertoire distinct from Central Javanese gamelan; the pelog degung scale (pentatonic) and the social function of the music — originally restricted to aristocratic courts but now democratized — demonstrate how 'gamelan' is not a single tradition but a family of distinct regional ones.

Flamenco's three core elements — cante (song), baile (dance), and toque (guitar playing) — exist in a specific hierarchical relationship in traditional flamenco: the singer (cantaor) is considered supreme, with the guitarist and dancer responding to and supporting the song; this hierarchy is frequently inverted in commercial flamenco performances for tourists.

Stockhausen's 'Gesang der Jünglinge' (1956) — combining a boy soprano's voice with electronically generated sounds — was the first masterpiece of electronic music, demonstrating that electronic technology could achieve the same emotional depth as acoustic instruments and laying the groundwork for all subsequent electronic music.

Music production has become increasingly 'in-the-box' (entirely within computer software) since the 2000s; a contemporary hit record can be produced entirely within a laptop using software like Ableton Live, Logic Pro, or FL Studio — democratizing music production while also homogenizing the sonic characteristics of contemporary pop.

The practice of 'looping' — recording a performance and immediately playing it back while adding new layers — was pioneered by jazz guitarist Les Paul in the 1940s using modified disc recorders and later tape, making him the father of multi-track recording, which became the universal standard of studio production.

The American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers (ASCAP), founded in 1914, was the first performing rights organization in the United States; its establishment followed years of composers including John Philip Sousa lobbying Congress for royalties when their music was performed in hotels and restaurants.

The 'Joni Mitchell effect' in music cognition refers to the phenomenon whereby a listener's experience of a well-known recording becomes so embedded in memory that hearing the same song covered or reinterpreted creates a dual perception — both the new performance and the remembered original — that enriches rather than replaces the prior experience.

Anti-apartheid singer Miriam Makeba — known as 'Mama Africa' — had her U.S. visa revoked in 1968 after she married Stokely Carmichael of the Black Panther Party; she lived in exile for 30 years, using her internationally celebrated status to bring the world's attention to South African apartheid.

Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan introduced qawwali to Western audiences through Peter Gabriel's WOMAD festivals in the late 1980s; his collaborations with Gabriel on the 'Last Temptation of Christ' soundtrack and with Eddie Vedder on the 'Dead Man Walking' soundtrack demonstrated that Sufi devotional music could cross cultural and spiritual boundaries.

The International Standard Recording Code (ISRC) — a 12-character alphanumeric code assigned to individual sound recordings and music videos — is the standard identifier used by streaming platforms, performing rights organizations, and copyright registries worldwide to track and distribute royalties to rights holders.

The global market for music merchandise — T-shirts, vinyl, posters, and other artist-branded physical goods — exceeded $3.5 billion annually by the early 2020s, becoming a critical revenue stream for artists at all levels as digital streaming revenue remains insufficient to support touring musicians' incomes.

John Williams — composer of the 'Star Wars,' 'Indiana Jones,' 'Schindler's List,' 'E.T.,' and 'Jaws' themes — has received 53 Academy Award nominations, the most for any living person and the second-most in Oscar history after Walt Disney; his themes are among the most recognized pieces of music globally.

source.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

text: The concept of 'music as medicine' is gaining scientific traction: the field of neurologic music therapy (NMT), developed at Colorado State University, uses specific music-based techniques with neurological evidence backing to treat conditions including stroke, Parkinson's, traumatic brain injury, and autism spectrum disorder.

The first concert ever live-streamed to a global internet audience was a Rolling Stones 'Voodoo Lounge' concert in 1994 — then cutting-edge technology watched by a few thousand people on primitive multimedia PCs; by 2020, single livestream events were attracting hundreds of millions of concurrent viewers.

The COVID-19 pandemic's closure of live music venues in 2020 caused an estimated $30 billion loss to the global live music industry; the crisis accelerated the development of virtual concert platforms and prompted regulatory debate about musician unemployment benefits in countries without robust social safety nets for freelance artists.

Ghana's 'highlife' pioneer Ebo Taylor, who remained relatively unknown outside West Africa for most of his career, gained international recognition in his 80s when DJs and producers rediscovered his 1970s recordings; his example is used in musicology to illustrate how European and American critical gatekeepers determine which African artists achieve 'global' fame.

The Chinese Communist Party's 'red songs' (hong ge) campaign — reviving revolutionary-era mass songs for patriotic education — shows how music remains an active tool of state ideology; 'Red Song' singing competitions and broadcasts have been required at schools and workplaces in periodic campaigns since the 1950s.

The Bonobo — a great ape closely related to chimpanzees — shows the most complex musical behavior of any non-human primate, spontaneously producing varied vocal sequences with interval structures that researchers have described as 'proto-melodic,' suggesting that the cognitive precursors of musical ability may predate the human lineage.

Music's capacity to cross linguistic barriers is evidenced by the global success of non-English language music: ABBA's Swedish-accented English, BTS's Korean lyrics, and Rosalía's Catalan flamenco-pop have all achieved massive English-speaking audiences, challenging the historic dominance of American English in global popular music.

The 'Payphone' by Maroon 5 (2012) was the first song in chart history to be certified Diamond (10 million copies sold/streamed) in the streaming era; the certification threshold was subsequently adjusted multiple times as streaming-to-sale conversions changed the economics of hit music.

The 'Maori Song Contest' — Te Matatini — held every two years in New Zealand, is the world's premier competition for Maori performing arts including waiata (song), haka, and poi; it draws over 40,000 spectators and has played a central role in the revitalization of Maori language and cultural performance.

Artificial intelligence music generation — systems like OpenAI's MuseNet, Google's MusicLM, and Suno AI — can now generate convincing multi-instrument compositions in specified styles from text prompts, raising profound questions about authorship, copyright, and the nature of musical creativity that copyright law has yet to fully address.

The 'music of the plants' experiments — in which electrodes attached to plants transduce their bioelectrical responses into audible sounds — have produced surprising results suggesting plants respond measurably to music; while scientifically contested, the concept has inspired artists including Mort Garson and forms part of the broader tradition of 'extended organism' music.

The global music education market — encompassing private lessons, online platforms, instrument sales, and formal music school tuition — was valued at over $30 billion annually by the early 2020s, driven by platform-based learning services like Simply Piano, Yousician, and Fender Play that democratized instrument instruction.

The concept of 'musical intelligence' — one of Howard Gardner's original eight 'multiple intelligences' proposed in 1983 — posited that musical ability is a distinct cognitive capacity separate from linguistic or logical-mathematical intelligence; while Gardner's framework is contested in psychology, it influenced music education philosophy significantly.

The Wangga song tradition of the Belyuen (Larrakia) people of the Northern Territory of Australia is one of the few Aboriginal music traditions with identified individual composers: songs are given to humans in dreams by spirit beings, meaning the composer is credited as receiver rather than creator — a fundamentally different conception of musical authorship.

source.name: Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies

text: The tradition of the 'rock and roll hall of fame inductee speech' has itself become a cultural institution: inductee speeches have featured reunions, surprise performances, political statements, and emotional public acknowledgments between artists whose relationships defined decades of music history.

source.name: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame

text: The 'Topline' in contemporary pop production refers to the melody and lyrics written over a pre-made instrumental track; the division between 'track makers' (beatmakers/producers) and 'topline writers' (melody and lyric specialists) has created a specialized professional category and complex multi-party copyright situations.

The Tuvan khoomei throat singing style has been studied by physicists who have demonstrated that skilled practitioners can independently control two or three resonant frequencies simultaneously — a degree of fine-motor control over the vocal tract that has no parallel in Western singing technique.

source.name: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America

text: The West African tradition of 'tonal language' drumming — in which drum tones mimic the pitch patterns of tonal languages to send messages — was the world's most sophisticated pre-electronic long-distance communication technology; Belgian colonizers attempted to ban it because they could not monitor communications between villages.

The 'Misty' jazz standard, composed by Erroll Garner in 1954, became a legal battleground in 1978 when the Supreme Court case Clint Eastwood's 'Play Misty for Me' (which used the song) was referenced in debates about copyright; the song's history illustrates how standard compositions become embedded in both musical tradition and legal precedent.

The pan-African Afrobeat genre that Fela Kuti created in the 1970s deliberately blended Yoruba musical traditions with James Brown-influenced funk to create a music he described as both artistically revolutionary and politically dangerous to Nigeria's military governments, who raided his communal home 'Kalakuta Republic' and imprisoned him multiple times.

Research in embodied music cognition shows that even passive music listening involves subtle motor activation — your motor cortex responds to a beat even when you are sitting still — explaining why it is physically difficult to remain completely motionless while listening to strongly rhythmic music.

Polyphonic overtone singing — in which a single vocalist produces a melody of upper harmonics over a drone — has been independently developed by Tuvan, Mongolian, Tibetan, Bashkir, and South African Xhosa singers, suggesting that the technique emerges naturally in cultures that value drone-based vocal traditions.

The practice of 'busking' (street performance) has a documented history stretching to ancient Rome and medieval Europe; modern buskers in cities like London and New York can earn up to $75,000 annually in busy locations, and successful busking careers have launched artists including Ed Sheeran and Tracy Chapman.

Music piracy via cassette tape was the first major copyright crisis facing the recorded music industry: the 'Home Taping is Killing Music' campaign of the 1980s claimed cassette home-copying was destroying record sales, though economists then and now argue that home tapers were also among music's most committed buyers.

The late Icelandic composer Jóhann Jóhannsson, known for the 'Arrival' and 'Arrival' soundtracks, exemplified the blurring of contemporary classical and film music in the 21st century; his approach — drawing equally from minimalism, neo-Romanticism, and electroacoustics — influenced a generation of hybrid composer-producers.

The concept of 'house music' as a spiritual practice is explicit in its origins: producers like Larry Heard (Mr. Fingers) and Frankie Knuckles consciously modeled house music on gospel — using the same structure of build, release, and transcendence — and described DJ-ing as 'a calling' equivalent to preaching.

Music festivals originated as religious and civic celebrations in ancient cultures — from Olympic Games musical competitions in ancient Greece to the harvest festivals of Mesopotamia; the secular commercial outdoor festival of the 20th century represents a transformation of this ancient communal function into an entertainment product.

The 'battle of the bands' format — amateur bands competing live for prizes and recording opportunities — was a standard grassroots industry development tool from the 1960s through the 1990s; it has largely been replaced by online streaming and social media as mechanisms for talent discovery.

The 'Afrobeats to the world' movement of the 2010s–2020s is supported by a specific diaspora network: African music promoters, club nights, and radio shows in London, New York, Toronto, and Paris created local markets that gave Nigerian and Ghanaian artists international toeholds before major label signing.

The Royal College of Music, founded in London in 1882, was one of the first institutions to offer professional music training to women on equal terms with men; its founding was partly motivated by the belief that women's participation in music would elevate the cultural life of the Empire.

The 'great vowel shift' in English pronunciation (1400–1700) changed how English-speaking singers and choir masters transmitted vocal technique; the resulting discrepancy between how English words are pronounced in speech versus sung — particularly in early music — continues to be a source of scholarly debate in historical performance practice.

source.name: Journal of the International Phonetic Association

text: Ligeti's 'Études' for piano (1985–2001) — 18 pieces exploring complex polyrhythms, cross-rhythms, and micropolyphony inspired by African music, Conlon Nancarrow, and fractal mathematics — are considered the most important contribution to piano literature since Chopin's études and among the most challenging concert works written for the instrument.

The Congolese guitar style known as sebene — a fast, rhythmic, interlocking guitar pattern forming the climax of soukous dance music — influenced guitar players across Africa and became a model for African popular music production; Franco (François Luambo Makiadi) is credited with developing and popularizing the style through thousands of recordings.

Ozzy Osbourne's 'Crazy Train' opens with one of rock music's most iconic riffs, played by guitarist Randy Rhoads — who died in a plane crash in 1982 at age 25; Rhoads had planned to leave rock music to pursue a classical guitar degree, and his brief but influential career is one of the great tragedies of rock history.

The 'singing voice' used by medieval troubadours in Occitania (southern France) — nasal, high, and with minimal vibrato — was radically different from modern classical vocal production; historical performance practice scholars have used medieval music theory texts, paintings, and poetic meter to reconstruct these lost vocal styles.

The 'music business royalties pyramid' means that for every dollar a consumer spends on streaming, approximately 52 cents goes to recording rights holders (mostly major labels), 15 cents to songwriters and publishers (mechanical royalties), and the remainder to platform operating costs — leaving artists at the end of a long chain of intermediaries.

The Paraguayan harp — a diatonic lap harp with 32–38 strings capable of playing in multiple keys through a technique of quickly retuning individual strings mid-performance — is the national instrument of Paraguay and is considered the most technically demanding of all Latin American folk harps.

source.name: Centro Cultural de la República del Paraguay

text: The concept of 'toasting' in Jamaican dancehall — in which a DJ improvises vocal commentary over a riddim (rhythm track) — is a direct ancestor of hip-hop's MC tradition; DJ Kool Herc, widely credited as hip-hop's founder, grew up in Jamaica and brought toasting and sound system culture to the Bronx.

The classical music canon — the standard repertoire performed by orchestras and taught in conservatories — was largely defined by Austrian and German critics in the 19th century; feminist and postcolonial musicologists have spent decades arguing that this canon systematically excludes women, non-European, and non-white composers.

source.name: Journal of the American Musicological Society

text: The 'balungan' in Javanese gamelan — the skeleton melody that each instrument ornaments in its own characteristic way — has no Western equivalent; it is not the tune but rather a structural framework around which different instruments improvise according to their register, timbre, and traditional role within the ensemble.

The acoustic properties of prehistoric caves — particularly reverberant chambers — appear to have been deliberately chosen as sites for cave paintings, suggesting that early humans may have used resonant rock surfaces as 'sound stages' and that the painted animals were visual accompaniments to ritual music and percussion.

source.name: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory

text: The development of the piano pedal — particularly the sustaining (damper) pedal — transformed piano music from the early 19th century onward; Beethoven's 'Moonlight Sonata' instruction 'senza sordino' (without dampers, meaning with the sustaining pedal held throughout the movement) creates an atmospheric blend of harmonies impossible on a modern piano.

The world record for the most people playing guitar simultaneously is 7,344, set at the Nürburgring in Germany in 2019 when Foo Fighters led a mass performance of 'Learn to Fly'; the event was originally staged as a fan-organized petition to convince the band to play in their city — demonstrating music's power to mobilize community action.

Berber music of the Atlas Mountains in Morocco — including the ahwach collective dance-song and the ahouach — is performed without a designated leader; all participants simultaneously sing, drum, and dance in a spontaneous collective process that makes traditional Western concepts of composer, performer, and audience inapplicable.

Improvised music traditions exist across every musical culture but take radically different forms: Western jazz improvisation works within chord changes; Indian classical improvisation explores a raga's melodic space; maqam improvisation in Middle Eastern music develops characteristic phrases; Tibetan ritual improvisation follows prescribed emotional intentions.

The 'Nashville Superstar' format of TV talent shows — from American Idol (2002) to The Voice (2011) to American Song Contest (2022) — has become the dominant mechanism for artist discovery in the mainstream music industry, though critics argue it prioritizes vocal technique and marketability over artistic innovation.

Music notation's 'grand staff' — two staves connected by a brace for piano, typically treble above and bass below — was standardized in the 19th century; before this, a wide variety of clef combinations were used, and organ tablature (which used numbers and letters rather than note-heads) was common in the Baroque era.

The 'long count' of Maya civilization included a ritualistic music calendar: specific instruments (turtle shell drums, conch trumpets, ocarinas) were associated with particular calendar periods, and musical performance was tied to astronomical events including Venus cycles that the Maya tracked with extraordinary precision.

source.name: Foundation for the Advancement of Mesoamerican Studies

text: The Irish traditional music revival of the 1960s — driven by Seán Ó Riada's Ceoltóirí Chualann ensemble and the subsequent Chieftains — reframed Irish traditional music as a sophisticated art music rather than rural entertainment, helping to reverse the stigma attached to traditional music by Irish urban middle classes in the postcolonial era.

The global pop song has converged on a standard format: 3–4 minutes, verse-chorus-verse-chorus-bridge-chorus structure, major or minor key, with a hook in the chorus — a format that is partly a product of radio play requirements, partly streaming's skip-rate optimization, and partly the dominance of Max Martin-influenced production school songwriting.

The music of Hildegard of Bingen has been more frequently recorded in the late 20th and 21st centuries than in all previous centuries combined, partly because feminist musicologists championed her as the earliest documented female composer, and partly because her unusual, soaring melodies suit new-age and early-music aesthetics.

The mbira's primary tuning in Zimbabwe — which varies by region and family — is considered personal, almost biological; a well-made mbira is said to be 'alive,' and traditional mbira makers refuse to tune instruments to external pitch standards, insisting each instrument has its own correct tuning determined by the materials and spirit of the maker.

source.name: Paul Berliner, The Soul of Mbira

text: The German opera tradition of 'Gesamtkunstwerk' (total work of art), advocated by Wagner, envisioned music, drama, poetry, visual art, and dance unified in a single artistic experience; this concept influenced theater, film, multimedia performance art, and 20th-century avant-garde forms from Brecht's theater to contemporary immersive opera.

Sonic branding — the creation of distinctive audio identities for corporations, including jingles, sonic logos, and custom music systems — has become a multi-billion dollar industry; research shows that audio branding increases brand recall by up to 96% compared to visual branding alone.

The tradition of 'busoni transcriptions' — Franz Liszt and Ferruccio Busoni's piano arrangements of Bach's organ works — created a repertoire of 'transcriptions' that are now themselves canonical; the concept that a transcription is itself an artistic act of interpretation, not merely a technical translation, fundamentally changed how musicians think about adaptation.

Music playlisting by Spotify's editorial team is deeply influential: a 'New Music Friday' or 'RapCaviar' feature can add millions of streams to a track within days; independent artists and labels spend significant resources attempting to reach playlist curators, creating a new tier of industry gatekeeping distinct from radio and traditional press.

Throat cancer forced Jack Bruce (Cream), Roger Ebert (film critic and music writer), and Édith Piaf to abandon or severely limit their singing careers; the physiological vulnerability of the human voice — the singing instrument is entirely organic tissue — means vocal careers are uniquely susceptible to illness, aging, and misuse.

The concept of 'rasa' (emotional essence) in Indian aesthetics, codified in the Nāṭyaśāstra, identifies eight (later nine) fundamental emotional states that art should evoke — including love, heroism, disgust, and tranquility — providing a theory of emotional aesthetics that predates Western psychology by nearly 2,000 years.

The tradition of musical instrument 'voices' — each string or wind instrument being described in anthropomorphic vocal terms (soprano recorder, alto flute, tenor saxophone, bass clarinet) — reflects Western music's deep connection between the human voice and instrument design, with vocal ranges used as the primary organizational framework.

The 'music of grief' (lament) occupies a special status across cultures: Greek epitaphs describe professional mourning women, Lamentations in the Hebrew Bible are organized as musical poems, and the global ubiquity of slow-tempo, minor-key music at funerals suggests that specific musical features universally signal and induce grief.

The Welsh national anthem 'Hen Wlad Fy Nhadau' (Land of My Fathers, 1856) was the first national anthem to be sung by a crowd at an international sporting event — at a Wales vs. New Zealand rugby match in 1905 — establishing the tradition of national anthem singing at sports events that is now universal.

India's national anthem 'Jana Gana Mana,' composed by Rabindranath Tagore in 1911, was initially suspected by British authorities of being a song praising King George V during his India visit; it was later adopted as the national anthem at independence in 1950 — a song whose colonial reception and post-colonial meaning are thus entirely reversed.

New Zealand's national anthem 'God Defend New Zealand' is officially performed in two stanzas — first in Maori (Te Aroha) and then in English — a bilingual policy adopted in 1977 that reflects the country's commitment to acknowledging its Treaty of Waitangi obligations; the two texts are not translations of each other.

The anthem 'Advance Australia Fair' became Australia's official national anthem only in 1984, after a public poll in 1977 — Waltzing Matilda, an unofficial national song about a sheep thief, received more votes than any anthem candidate in informal surveys, reflecting Australians' sardonic relationship with official national symbolism.

The concept of 'found sound' in music — using environmental and accidental sounds as compositional material — was systematized by Pierre Schaeffer, extended by John Cage, and has now become mainstream in hip-hop production, film scoring, and electronic music; everyday objects from refrigerator hums to traffic noise have appeared in commercially released music.

Ethnomusicologist Bruno Nettl proposed a universal set of musical 'universals' including the use of scales, the marking of cultural boundaries through music, and the existence of music in all human societies — though subsequent research has refined and contested each of these, the debate itself has been productive for understanding music's biological and cultural bases.

source.name: Bruno Nettl, The Study of Ethnomusicology

text: The Scottish 'ceili' (ceilidh) — an informal dance event with live traditional music — serves not just as entertainment but as a social bonding mechanism; research on community ceilidhs shows significantly elevated self-reported social connection and wellbeing compared to equivalent non-musical gatherings.

The concept of 'extended technique' in classical music — non-standard playing methods that produce unusual sounds — includes col legno (bowing with the wood of the bow), sul ponticello (bowing very close to the bridge), and harmonics; these techniques, once considered radical, are now standard parts of orchestral and chamber music writing.

The 'Music for Sustainable Development' program of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization recognizes music as a tool for achieving Sustainable Development Goals — documenting cases where traditional music preservation supports biodiversity knowledge, community resilience, and mental health across developing nations.

The Congolese sapeur community — elegant men and women who dedicate significant income to designer clothing — celebrates their lifestyle through the music of Papa Wemba, whose recordings explicitly praised dandyism as a form of dignity and resistance against poverty; the fusion of music, fashion, and identity politics makes sapeur culture a uniquely rich object of sociological study.

The music industry's shift to 'streaming economy' has created a new underclass of 'micro-celebrities' — artists with dedicated fan bases of tens of thousands who generate sustainable income through a combination of streaming, merchandise, Patreon, and live shows without ever achieving mainstream chart success.

The phenomenon of 'dead concerts' — Grateful Dead performances that fans were encouraged to record and freely circulate — created one of the first examples of music as a 'gift economy,' predating the internet's sharing culture by decades and establishing a devoted fan community (Deadheads) whose tape-trading networks later influenced the online file-sharing culture.

source.name: Grateful Dead Archive, UC Santa Cruz

text: The concept of musical 'groove' — the sensation of wanting to move in response to rhythm — has been studied by music psychologist Justin London and shown to be maximized when rhythmic patterns are complex enough to create expectation violations but regular enough to remain predictable; the 'sweet spot' of rhythmic complexity that produces groove is culture-specific.

Music literacy — the ability to read and write musical notation — has declined significantly in popular music: most contemporary pop and rock musicians work entirely by ear, via recordings, or using chord notation rather than standard notation; this shift parallels how digital photography reduced the need for darkroom technical skills.

The 'concert experience' has been transformed by smartphone use: while audience phones light up entire arenas at concerts — replacing lighters as a visual spectacle — artists including Alicia Keys, Jack White, and Adele have banned phones at concerts to restore undivided attention, arguing phones mediate experience rather than enhance it.

Tabla construction requires the baking ('sintering') of a black circular paste (syahi) on the right drum head, made from a mixture of iron powder, flour, and other materials in a process unique to each maker; this syahi takes years of playing to season properly and is what gives the tabla its distinctive harmonic, bell-like tone.

The 'indie game' music revolution — pioneered by composers like Darren Korb (Bastion, Transistor), Austin Wintory (Journey), and Disasterpeace (Fez) — created a new aesthetic in game music that explicitly rejected orchestral blockbuster convention in favor of genre hybrids, ambient textures, and folk-influenced composition.

The 'copyright troll' phenomenon in music — in which entities buy catalogs of obscure copyrights specifically to sue YouTube users and content creators — has generated hundreds of millions in settlements and led to YouTube's ContentID automated copyright detection system, which itself has been criticized for suppressing legitimate uses of music.

Music's relationship to memory storage is unique: while episodic memories (events) and semantic memories (facts) deteriorate with Alzheimer's, procedural musical memory — the muscle memory of playing an instrument — can survive to late stages of the disease, allowing patients who can no longer speak to still play pieces they learned decades earlier.

The 'protest music paradox' — the observation that commercially successful protest music often loses its subversive power by entering the mainstream — has been documented in the co-optation of Bob Dylan, The Clash, and Rage Against the Machine; playing their protest anthems in advertisements or political campaigns they would have opposed illustrates how capitalism absorbs its cultural critics.

The 'Internationale' contains one of music history's more remarkable copyright stories: the original melody was composed in 1888 by Pierre De Geyter, who transferred his rights to the French Workers' Party; after 70 years of copyright dispute with his brother, the melody entered the public domain across most of the world in the 1950s–60s.

The phrase 'elevator music' entered common usage in the 1940s and 1950s when Muzak Corporation was actively installed in elevators; the term now functions as a pejorative for any music considered bland, inoffensive, and interchangeable — though musicologists note this dismissal rarely extends to equally generic music in other approved contexts.

The Yoruba 'dundun' (talking drum) ensemble traditionally requires at least seven years of apprenticeship with a master before a player is considered competent; the instrument's capacity to mimic Yoruba tonal language with fine precision requires learning not just drumming technique but the tonal structure of the language itself.

source.name: Journal of the Society for American Music

text: The global K-pop fandom culture — characterized by intense parasocial relationships, organized streaming campaigns, and multilingual community organizing — represents a new form of music consumption in which fans are active participants in an artist's career metrics rather than passive consumers, deliberately manipulating charts and streaming numbers.

The first sound recording ever made — and the oldest surviving human voice recording — is a 10-second excerpt of the French folk song 'Au Clair de la Lune,' recorded on a 'phonautograph' by Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville in Paris in 1860, predating Edison's phonograph by 17 years; the recording was not intended to be played back and was rediscovered in 2008.

The accordion — brought to the Americas by European immigrants in the 19th century — has become essential to dozens of distinct regional genres: Cajun zydeco, Colombian vallenato, Mexican norteño, Argentine tango, Polish polka, and Irish ceili music all feature the accordion despite having no historical connection to each other.

Research on 'cultural music surprise' — the acoustic shock of encountering radically unfamiliar musical systems — shows that while first exposure to Bulgarian parallel harmony, Indian microtonality, or Tuvan throat singing often produces discomfort in Western listeners, repeated exposure rapidly normalizes and even generates appreciation, suggesting musical taste is highly plastic.

The 'Grateful Dead economy' — in which fan-generated content, tape trading, and concert ticket income replaced record sales as the band's primary revenue stream — was decades ahead of its time and anticipated the direct-to-fan digital economy that eventually transformed the music industry.

Composer Arvo Pärt's 'tintinnabuli' technique — developed in the 1970s as a mystical compositional method in which a 'tintinnabuli voice' arpegiates a tonic triad while a 'melodic voice' moves stepwise through the scale — creates music of extreme austerity and devotional intensity that has made him one of the most-performed living composers.

Bandcamp, founded in 2008, became the dominant direct-to-fan music platform by allowing artists to set their own prices and keep 85–90% of revenue; 'Bandcamp Fridays' during the COVID-19 pandemic, in which Bandcamp waived its fees entirely, generated millions of dollars for independent artists and became a model of platform solidarity.

Music's capacity to build community across social divisions has been demonstrated in countless peace-building programs: the West-Eastern Divan Orchestra, founded by Daniel Barenboim and Edward Said in 1999 and comprising Israeli, Palestinian, and Arab musicians, uses musical collaboration as a platform for dialogue and a concrete example of coexistence.

The Sufi music tradition of qawwali includes a practice called 'hal' — a state of spiritual ecstasy triggered by a particularly moving passage of music, in which the listener may weep, shout, or become physically still; this state is considered evidence of divine grace and is the goal of devotional musical performance.

The 'song camp' model — week-long intensive songwriting retreats where teams of writers and producers collaborate to create commercially targeted music — has become the dominant production method for major-label pop; songs are written by committees for specific artists' 'brand voices,' raising philosophical questions about authenticity in popular music.

The practice of 'musical exorcism' — using percussion, chanting, and ritual music to drive out malevolent spirits or cure mental illness — is documented in ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, and China, and continues in modified forms in healing ceremonies in many contemporary indigenous cultures.

The Argentine national anthem, adopted in 1813, features some of the most martial and violent lyrics of any national anthem — calling for 'thundering cannons' to 'crown the nation with glory' — yet its official performance at the 2014 FIFA World Cup required a specially approved shorter version to fit broadcast timing constraints.

The 'Ode to Joy' theme from Beethoven's Ninth Symphony has been adopted as the anthem of the European Union — in an orchestral arrangement without Friedrich Schiller's original German lyrics — chosen for its message of universal brotherhood and its status as the most internationally recognized classical theme.

The American folk revival of the 1960s was partly engineered: folk impresario Harold Leventhal, Sing Out! Magazine, and the Newport Folk Festival deliberately promoted folk music as a political-cultural alternative to commercial pop, in the process helping to launch the careers of Bob Dylan, Joan Baez, Phil Ochs, and Peter, Paul and Mary.

The 'feedback loop' between music and language is documented across multiple dimensions: listening to music in a second language improves language learning outcomes; learning to read music has been shown to improve reading of written text; and bilingual children show superior musical pitch discrimination — suggesting music and language share more cognitive infrastructure than previously thought.

The global market for musical instruments was valued at approximately $17 billion in 2023, with the guitar remaining the best-selling instrument category; during the COVID-19 pandemic, guitar and piano sales surged as homebound people took up instruments — a 'pandemic music revival' that echoed the home music-making culture of the pre-recording era.

The most performed choral work in history is arguably George Frideric Handel's 'Messiah,' performed annually in hundreds of cities worldwide since its 1741 premiere; the tradition of audience members standing for the 'Hallelujah' chorus, the work's consistent role in charitable fundraising, and its continued status as a living communal ritual make it the single most enduring example of music binding community across time.
